I would **not submit Ryan’s row as though the issue were settled**. I’d immediately seek a temporary hold on his row and the automatic termination letter, and urgently alert HR and payroll for a human decision before noon. I’d submit the other entries as usual and make sure Ryan’s row is tracked for prompt resolution—not silently dropped.

On the facts and definitions provided, SC is inaccurate because Ryan says he was not ill. DEP does not fit the stated definition: his sister is not one of the listed relatives and does not live in his household. BRV does not apply. So **UA appears to be the code under the literal rules**. His call to Gary does not make the absence booked in advance, but it is relevant: he gave notice and describes an emergency. He should not be asked for evidence when the policy says none is required.

Because a second UA triggers a same-day dismissal letter, I would not let an automated consequence issue without urgent human review of how the rule applies here. I would not relabel the absence as SC or DEP just to avoid that outcome, and I would not rely on a free-text note to prevent it—the note has no effect on payroll or probation. I’d preserve a concise factual record and, once an authorized person decides, apply the correct code and arrange any necessary payroll correction.
